But if that were the case, I probably wouldn't be making it. I do get fun out of making the podcast. I learn a lot, don't get me wrong. But there are priorities, right? And I could do more research and I could write more books if I weren't doing the podcast. And if there were no monetary incentive whatsoever, maybe I'd still be doing it, I don't know for sure, but the incentive to do it would be less, let's put it that way. And if what I did was just put out there and instantly rebranded and stolen by somebody else, I would probably be making less money. And that's nothing compared to people who really have bestselling books or big movies or whatever. I'm in favor of incentivizing people to do good creative things, and I think that protection for intellectual property rights does that to some extent. I do think, like I said, it goes too far. Like, I don't know the details about this, but my impression is the estate of Albert Einstein exerts enormous control over when you can use a picture of Albert Einstein and things like that, which is a little silly. He died over 50 years ago, and they're not him, so what right do they have to do that? Would be my take, but again, I haven't thought it through carefully. Happy to hear important arguments on either side.

segments.questionText: Is it possible that if Mindscape AMAs ran for another billion years, you would one day stop saying yes to most questions that start with 'Is it possible that'?
segments.answerText: Yes, it is possible that. Mindscape AMAs are not gonna run for another billion years. I don't think that's actually possible. So let me just say two things here about this ongoing joke that we have here on Mindscape, that the answer to "Is it possible" questions is always yes. First, of course there are loopholes. Of course there are questions that are purely about logic. Is it possible that, according to the axioms of Euclidean geometry, a triangle on a plane Euclidean two-dimensional surface has interior angles that add up to 183 degrees? No, that is not possible. That's a mathematical thing, right? We cannot actually wriggle our way out of that given those assumptions that were buried into the question. The "Is it possible that" questions are always referring to science questions, because in science we have to keep an open mind. But there's a reason why I keep telling the joke in that way, it's always, you always say yes to "Is it possible that" questions, because I think that people don't really mean "Is it possible that X or Y is true" in the literal sense of it being possible. I think that people have an impression, which I don't think is a good impression to have, that if something's possible, then it's plausible, or even worse, that if it's possible, then it's worth spending time thinking about, right? "Is it possible that this theory is on the right track?" Sure, it's possible. That doesn't mean you should spend any time thinking about that particular theory. So part of the program, part of the ambition of constantly saying yes, it's possible, is just to nudge people toward being better Bayesian reasoners and to graduate from thinking, "Well, it's possible, therefore it's worthwhile, to really thinking about how much credence they put on these different things." There's very, very different degrees of possibility. Something having a 10 to the minus 100 chance of being true and something having a 10 to the minus 1 chance of being true are both possible, but they are not equally deserving of your attention.

segments.questionText: I was pleasantly surprised to hear on one of the last AMAs that your favorite time-wasting mobile games are the Kingdom Rush series, as these are also pretty much the only ones I play. I'm curious what difficulty setting you prefer, since my favorite part of these kinds of games is playing on the hardest difficulty and slowly figuring out the right placement and sequence of towers to beat each level. It turns a silly mobile game into a surprisingly satisfying problem-solving experience. I'm wondering if you do something similar or prefer to play on an easier difficulty where you can more or less just shut your brain off.
segments.answerText: No, actually, I also play on the hardest difficulty, and I think that there's an interesting balance here. If the game were just something where I won every time without trying very hard, that wouldn't be that interesting. But also if it's too hard, if I have to put too much brain power into thinking about how to do it and practicing and doing many, many, many times before I beat it, that's also not what I want out of my silly little iPad game. So I think that usually Kingdom Rush gets it right. There are some levels, et cetera, that are harder than they should be and it's just annoying. There are plenty of ones that are easy, but that's okay. To mix in some easy ones and some hard ones is just about right. You don't want to put brain power at all into it every single time. But I do think that... I think that the later editions of the game have actually become too complicated. There's too many moving parts, too many towers and heroes and whatever. And I'm like, I don't want to think about all that. That's not really why I'm there. I want to do a little bit of thinking. That's why it's hard for me to complain too legitimately, because I do want to do some thinking, just not too much.

segments.questionText: After recently reading Brian Greene's The Hidden Reality, I've been thinking more about the different physical theories that imply a multiverse. I know you have a very high credence in many-worlds and a relatively low credence in Max Tegmark's Level 4 multiverse, where all mathematical structures correspond to a physical reality. I'm curious where you stand on the various other physical theories that lead to the multiverse. Since I cannot ask all that here, I'll simply ask your credence on the multiverse implied by eternal inflation. I know it is lower than many-worlds and greater than Level 4, but can you provide a bit more color on exactly how serious we should take eternal inflation?
segments.answerText: Yeah, for eternal inflation, I'm just gonna totally weasel out here and put my credence at about 0.5, at about 50%, which is the least informative answer that I can give. If I said it was 0.1, that would say I really think it's probably not there. If I said 0.9, I probably would think that it is there. 0.5 says I just don't know. And that's because there are really good arguments on both sides, existence and non-existence. On the pro-existence side, we have the fact that inflation is very useful for accounting for the initial conditions we see in our universe, and inflation tends to typically be eternal in many models. That's a speculative question. People don't necessarily agree on that, but that is a very plausible reading of the whole thing. And out of that, you can get a multiverse that has explanatory power for things like the value of the vacuum energy in our universe, et cetera. So it's kind of a nice picture that you get. On the minus side, number one, it absolutely invokes completely ill-understood regimes of physics, energies and times and things like that that we have no direct evidence of. So we should be not very tied to any specific theories. We should be kind of open-minded. And secondly, there's real problems with eternal inflation. There's the measure problem, there's the predictability problem, there's the entropy problem of the early universe. I think that... The fact that... If you really truly believe the naive picture of the multiverse, it's very hard to say what it predicts because everything happens an infinite number of times. Everything that can happen at all happens an infinite number of times. And you might want to say, "Okay, but some things happen twice as often as other things." That's your intuition, but that turns out to be very hard to make careful and rigorous. It's just very hard to say that certain things happen twice as often as other things, and therefore it's very hard to make predictions. And I think that people who believe in inflation have mostly swept that under the rug and ignored it, and I think they should pay closer attention to it. In fact, just saying this out loud makes me think I should include that in the colloquium I'm planning to give soon that I mentioned other things I think physicists should think about. So I should include the cosmological measure problem as one of them.

segments.questionText: Regarding your time in New Mexico, red, green, or Christmas?
segments.answerText: Usually red, but sometimes Christmas just to mix things up. These, of course, if you don't know, these refer to colors of chili that you put on your meal. All sorts of meals can be covered with various kinds of chili sauce. And they can either be red chili, green chili, or Christmas means half and half, red and green. Get it? Christmas. So I went for the Christmas for a long time, but I think I do enjoy the red usually more than the green.

segments.questionText: What can we say about the interior of a black hole by studying its event horizon, taking into account the holographic principle, in particular by doing practical observations from Earth?
segments.answerText: Well, I think that the cheap and correct answer is nothing, [chuckle] in the sense that if you mean... I should have grouped this together with the question about is there evidence for the multiverse, 'cause it's a very spiritually similar question. You can't see in the interior of a black hole. You cannot get data from the interior of a black hole by any observation that you can do practically here on Earth. Open and shut case. What you can do, though, is have a comprehensive theory that predicts something about the interior of a black hole, and it also predicts something observable about the exterior of the black hole. And then if you get data about that, you can infer the existence of this unobservable thing inside. Again, it's exactly what the logic is for the many-worlds interpretation of quantum mechanics. You cannot observe these other worlds. Why do you think they're there? Well, because they are predicted very strongly on the basis of equations that are observable. The equations, the Schrödinger equation, entanglement, decoherence, these are all observable things, and they predict the existence of other worlds. So I think that the usual story about the interior of a black hole is we need to understand the theory, and then we should be able to predict what happens with good confidence. But that theory means not just general relativity, but also quantum gravity and other interesting quantum things that we don't have a great handle on quite yet.

segments.questionText: Could you please explain what superdeterminism means? I can't quite understand whether it's a standalone interpretation of quantum mechanics, and I can't wrap my head around the articles I've read. They immediately jump into Bell's theorem and describe the superdeterminism as a loophole in it.
segments.answerText: Right. So superdeterminism is an attempt to restore locality to quantum mechanics. And the reason why they always jump right into Bell's theorem is because Bell's theorem is the result that says that there is apparently violation of locality in quantum measurement. That when I measure something here, if it's entangled with something far away, there's an instantaneous change that has to be nonlocal. That's why they jump right into Bell's theorem. But superdeterminism itself is easy to state. Various results like Bell's theorem tell you what can and cannot happen on the basis of doing certain measurements, right? In quantum mechanics, you do measurements, you get results. And determinism is just the idea that, well, there is some initial state of the universe, and if in principle you knew the initial state, like if you're an Everettian, you could run the wave function of the universe through the Schrödinger equation and get it to predict everything that's gonna happen. That's determinism. Superdeterminism says, okay, that determinism, plus the initial conditions of the universe are really delicately set up so that certain observations never get made. [chuckle] So the reason why they jump right to Bell's theorem is that an assumption to Bell's theorem, or an assumption to make Bell's theorem relevant, is that I can do any observation I want. I can imagine measuring the spin along the x-axis or the y-axis or the z-axis, or any angle in between, et cetera, et cetera, right? And that's certainly allowed. But superdeterminism comes along and says, "Ah, but you are part of the physical universe. Your choices as to what experiments to do are secretly encoded in the initial conditions of the universe." And they take advantage of this loophole to say, "And the initial conditions of the universe are such that you think the Bell inequalities are being violated like they are in conventional quantum mechanics, even though strictly speaking, everything's perfectly local, you just can't notice it because you're never gonna do that experiment. To most people, this seems entirely wacky. But I can't use the wackiness argument myself because to many people, many worlds seems entirely wacky. The better argument for me is that many worlds just seems very simple and robust and what instantly falls into your lap once you understand entanglement. Superdeterminism seems like the opposite of that. It seems like a whole bunch of special pleading and crazy building of superstructure to avoid a result that is really just staring you in the face.

segments.questionText: Do you think large organizations like governments and corporations could qualify as an abstract form of life? Do you think the ideas, ideologies, or narratives could qualify as life? And can you imagine any other abstracts that might fit this definition?
segments.answerText: Well, if you go back to the podcast we did long ago with Stuart Bartlett, he and his friend... Was it Michael Wong? Was Michael Wong his collaborator? I think maybe he was, put forward this idea that they called lyfe, which I don't like the pronunciation of, but it's spelled L-Y-F-E. I very much like the spirit behind what they were trying to do, which is to say, forget about life. Forget about defining what is and is not life. It's very much in the spirit of the free will discussion. Forget about that. Talk about what are the characteristics that living systems usually have. They process information, they reproduce, they have homeostatic responses to external stimuli. They have a whole list, like seven different things that living life as we know it includes. And then they ask the question, could you imagine systems that have some of those features but not others? And the answer is very often, yes, you could. So rather than saying, is an organization qualifying as life, I would rather say, what are the various characteristics that life has? Which one of those are shared by large organizations? Some of them are, some of them are not. So I think that's... And I don't want to go through the list, but you can imagine going through the list yourself. I think that's a more intellectually satisfying question to ask. The thing I would say, though, is there is again a question of time scales, just like we bumped into when talking about why consciousness only sees one moment of time or one branch of the wave function. The brain, the human brain, is small enough and the electrochemical signals inside are rapid enough that the brain can act more or less coherently. Right? Your brain can do something all at once, roughly speaking. It doesn't take that long for the brain to get its act together and to organize all the different parts of the brain toward a common goal. Something like a large organization or a government, I don't think has that property. The different parts talk to each other, but they don't talk to each other fast enough and they don't organize fast enough to respond to the various things that happen to them. So that is one reason why I would not be overly tempted to identify an organization, a corporation, a government, whatever, as a living organism. I don't think it quite has that interactive coherence that I want my organisms to have. And this is likewise why when people say, "Could the galaxy be alive?" Or whatever. No. It's just things are too far apart. It's a very, very basic scientific limiting factor.

segments.questionText: What is your guess for the most recent modern discovery in fundamental physics that could have in principle been discovered by the ancient Greeks? For example, given the technology they had access to, could the Greeks have discovered the wave properties of light if they'd been looking in the right direction?
segments.answerText: No, I don't think so. The real difficulty there, maybe there's something clever that I can't think of very much, but they didn't have the ability... Sorry, let me back up. We had trouble discovering the wave properties of light in the modern world, right? Newton and Huygens completely disagreed about it. It really wasn't until the 19th century that we nailed that one down. And it was the double-slit experiment by Thomas Young. And the double-slit experiment in its classical form, forget about the quantum mechanical version, just the classical form, send a wave through two slits, they'll have an interference pattern on the other side. It only works if your wave is relatively coherent, right? It has the same amplitude and... Not the same amplitude, but the same wavelength and things like that. Setting up the double-slit experiment is harder than it looks. You could have made arguments like Newton and Huygens did. The ancient Greeks could have made similar arguments. They didn't have quite the technology. I don't know if they had the kind of glass that you could use to make a prism like Newton did, et cetera. But maybe they could have made arguments, but those arguments would not have been at all definitive. I think if you want to imagine what the Greeks could have done earlier, relativity is maybe a better guess, because they could have certainly invented the principle of relativity. Galileo did, right? And he was thinking about dropping cannonballs from moving ships in the harbor and stuff like that. And the Greeks knew all about that. So the Greeks absolutely could have invented the principle of relativity, conservation of momentum, things like that. Conservation of momentum didn't really come along until the Islamic Golden Age, like circa the year 1000. But the Greeks could have invented it; they just didn't. And if you have conservation of momentum, that is to say, in the absence of friction and air resistance and things like that, particles would move, or objects would move at a constant velocity, Newton's first law, then that plus relativity could get you the idea of relativity. It wouldn't give you special relativity because you don't know about the speed of light. You don't know about Maxwell's equations. You don't know there's any reason to think that the speed of light is constant in all frames. I'm not sure that they could have reasoned their way into thinking that. Could they have done something like the Michelson-Morley experiment? Probably not. The technology was not that great for the ancient Greeks, I gotta say. So I think that most of what we think of as "modern physics" really requires more technology than the Greeks had. They absolutely could have done classical mechanics; they could have done Newtonian mechanics. They just didn't have any reason to because they didn't have any experience experimentally with things moving at constant velocities, et cetera. Galileo showed them how you could do that with very little technology. So they could have done it, but they didn't really quite have the motivation for that.

segments.questionText: Why is entropy not considered a force? In my head, almost everything emerges from entropy, including the actual forces and gravity. Why is this the wrong way to think about it? Is this what came first, the chicken or the egg type of scenario?
segments.answerText: Well, sadly, this is a theme of this month's podcast, but it depends on what you mean by force, right? It depends on the definition. It used to be, back in the day, forces were defined operationally as things that gave rise to accelerations, right? F=ma. Why is something accelerating? Well, because there's a force acting on it. Now, in modern quantum field theory, of course, this has slightly changed its definition because we had gravity and we had electromagnetism, and those were the two best understood forces, and those are both described by gauge theories in quantum mechanics or quantum field theory, or even classically, for that matter. And so when it came along that we invented the strong and weak nuclear forces and those were also defined by gauge theories, we started saying there are four forces. Because what we really meant is there are four gauge theories, and gravity is not the same kind of gauge theory as the other three, but it's close enough to lump it into that bucket. That's not exactly the sort of Newtonian definition of force. It's really a much more narrow conception. If you go back to that sort of old-school Newtonian definition, then there's absolutely other forces of nature that are very relevant. When I am placing my coffee cup on the table in front of me, the thing that holds the coffee cup up is not electromagnetism, much less gravity or the nuclear forces. It's the degeneracy pressure. It's the exclusion principle from the atomic orbitals in the matter that is making up the coffee cup and the table. That's not listed among one of the four forces, but it's absolutely important for thinking about forces in our everyday lives. The reason I'm saying all this is just to point out that there's a little bit of "it's up to you" when you say, like, "Does this count as a force or does that count as a force?" There is absolutely an idea called entropic forces, and they are, what is the right way to say it? They're distinguished from mechanical forces. I think I talk a little bit about this in the Complexity and Emergence book that will be coming out at the probably the beginning of 2027. A mechanical force is when you literally have some system that has a potential energy that depends on its size or location, right? Like a spring has a mechanical force, and if you stretch it, it'll want to stretch back. If you compress it, it'll want to push back. An entropic force doesn't have any mechanical pushing or pulling, but it's a system that has a favorite size based on its entropy. Like if instead of a spring, if you have a very, very low-mass chain, you have little links in a chain, but they're very low-mass. They could just lay on the floor and they would exert no force whatsoever. But then you heat up the chain, so now it has a temperature, okay? And now the links in the chain are bouncing around and you can calculate the entropy of any given configuration of the links in the chain. And if you try to squeeze the chain to too small a region, it pushes back because there's more entropy if it's extended. But if you pull it, it also pushes back, because if you pull the chain to be completely straight, that has fewer accessible states and therefore lower entropy. So that is the idea of an entropic force, and it's different than a mechanical force. But I don't think that we have much good reason to think that all forces are entropic. As far as we know, there really are mechanical forces out there in the world. Since we don't know the theory of everything, that might change. But as of our current best understandings of things like gravity, electromagnetism, et cetera, these are mechanical forces, not entropic ones.

segments.questionText: I recently finished reading your book Quanta and Fields. If observations are what cause the wave function to collapse, then assuming the early universe began as only quantum fields, what caused those early quantum fields to collapse into particles with definitive states and properties?
segments.answerText: Well, if you're really interested in collapse of the wave function and all the philosophical issues of the measurement problem, et cetera, Quanta and Fields was not the book to read. It is an important book to read, but you should also read Something Deeply Hidden to really get into what happens when a measurement occurs, et cetera. It has nothing to do with measurements. It has nothing to do with observations, with consciousness, with awareness, with intelligence, with agency or anything like that. It's all just physics. It's all ultimately just the Schrödinger equation and what becomes entangled with what. Now, in the early universe, it is some work to decide what counts as the system and what counts as the environment. If you're looking at Schrödinger's cat, it's pretty straightforward. The cat's the system, all the particles in the air and the light in the photons are the environment, and there's that clear-cut distinction so you can say when decoherence happens. There's an ongoing attempt to figure out what is the best way to divide the early universe into system and environment. I even wrote a paper about that with Kim Boddy and Jason Pollack. And how it affects eternal inflation. But ultimately it doesn't matter that much. We want to know what we're going to see at the end of the day, including in the microwave background or something like that. And the way the quantum mechanics works is when you attach words like wave function collapse or decoherence or whatever, doesn't matter as long as you're just solving the Schrödinger equation overall. You can wait until the very last second to say what is being seen by this observer in the universe, and you will always get the same answer even if you sort of used the vocabulary of decoherence at earlier times. So, roughly speaking, it's the rest of the universe. Any given one particle interacts with all the other fields in the universe, and it becomes useful to talk about them when they're becoming entangled with the rest of the universe. But the details also matter, and those are a little bit slippery in the early universe period.

segments.questionText: about Jason Arday and says, "Should academic standards apply equally to everyone regardless of race?
segments.answerText: " Sure, they should. Yeah, that's an easy question. For those of you who don't know, Jason Arday was a Cambridge professor of education, maybe, or sociology. I don't know the details. I didn't follow the case very carefully. But he was accused of plagiarism, and he was pretty obviously guilty of plagiarism. And he was a Black guy. And so the accusations weren't just that he was a plagiarist, but that he was hired for his race rather than his scholarship, et cetera. And the right-wing sides of the British press hounded him to the point where he resigned from his position, and eventually he... Well, he died. It is thought that he committed suicide, but I'm not sure how clear that is. So it's kind of a tragic story in some ways. So on the one hand, it's very easy to say academic standards should apply equally to everyone regardless of race. It's also very easy to say that all sorts of standards are not applied equally to everyone regardless of race. There are cases, and I'm not going to go through them, you can look them up, there are cases here in the United States of prominent White academics who are very clearly committing research fraud and yet still have their jobs and their cushy gigs and things like that. So I don't think that the injustice is that somehow a Black guy got a job. I think that we don't apply standards of academic rectitude equally to people of different races, and that's kind of too bad.

segments.questionText: I'm starting my second year of a PhD in EHEP.
segments.answerText: I presume that's Experimental High Energy Physics. "In between my master's and PhD, I worked in industry for four years. I left industry because fundamental physics is my primary passion, and I've always wanted to pursue a career in academia HEP research. I recently received several job offers from recruiters, one of which is at a national research lab. It's very physics research focused, and if I were to leave academia, I could see it becoming a lifelong career that I'm content with. It also pays well, 175k per year. I want to finish my PhD and pursue a career studying fundamental physics, but as a broke grad student, this is very tempting. Additionally, I'm told that many people must spend six years in postdoc programs before they have a serious shot at a professorship, and many end up leaving academia anyway. I would really appreciate some perspective and advice. What would you say if one of your students came to you with this question, and did you ever consider leaving academia?" Yeah, I definitely considered leaving academia at various points in my career when it was not clear that I would have a successful job. One's employability as an academic goes up and down depending on what papers one has written recently, and that can be not a straight line upward or downward. So, happily, I was always in a position where, for the most part, not only did I have job offers, but I had more than one. So I could be pretty happy in taking the jobs that I was offered. Again, there's no way for me to answer this question for your particular situation. It depends a lot on things that I don't know about your career, what your research has been, what kind of things you're studying, et cetera. I'll say a bunch of things that are true, and you can take them into consideration as you go. Like I said before, most people who get PhDs, even from the very best places, are not able to become tenured professors. And you can just kind of obviously see that by the numbers game, right? In a physics department, many professors are graduating a student every year, but they don't retire every year. So what happens to those students? There's just not enough room for them. Philosophy departments try much harder to make sure that a large fraction of graduating PhD students do get jobs as professional philosophers, and as a result, we accept far, far fewer students into the graduate programs. But the reason why it's not a moral catastrophe for the physics departments to accept so many students is precisely because of situations like yours, where even if you don't get a job as a physics professor, you get some other job, typically that pays better than being a physics professor. And so I would say a couple things. It's hard to get a job. Don't be surprised if you don't as a tenured professor. Number two, it depends a lot on what kind of research you're doing. Is it the kind that departments are looking for in new professors, or is it something that is particular to you and you think is fascinating, but the rest of the world is not that interested in? What do you think your letters of recommendation are going to look like? Do you think that the people who are senior to you and going to be writing for you are really enthusiastic about your candidacy and will push you hard, or are they going along with it and trying to support you, but not actually really thinking that you're going to be a star someday? Also very important to think is how happy would you be in this other job? Maybe if it's not the absolute favorite job that you want, you could still make a good career out of it. And if you're making that kind of money to start, it sounds like you could be making a lot of money down the road. But on the other hand, on the fourth hand or whatever it is, if that job is there now, maybe a similar job is going to be there in a few years once you've gotten your PhD, right? And there's absolutely a case to be made for, if you do want to become a physics professor or professor of any kind, giving it your best shot and then seeing what happens. The great thing about a physics PhD is it does prepare you to do a whole bunch of different things, so you won't be out on the street at the end of it. So what I say to my own students is I can give you my feelings for probabilities, but the choice is ultimately yours. You have to do whatever it is your passion tells you to do. Like my very first graduate student who I graduated didn't even try to get academic jobs. He went right into consulting. Other people have tried for many years and struggled, and it's been hard. I've had a lot of luck recently with my students getting faculty jobs, but it comes and goes. The numbers are small and it's unpredictable, and academia as a whole, especially here in the United States, is not in a great position right now. So take all those things into consideration. All I can do is wish you luck. David asks a priority question. He says, "When using Bayes' theorem for updating your beliefs on a particular subject matter, whether it's are we a Boltzmann brain, is the many-worlds interpretation the correct interpretation of quantum mechanics, is God real? Et cetera, how do you frame those internally using Bayes' theorem? Do you have a specific probability that you handicap the subject matter in question and move the percentages in either direction every time you get a new piece of information to update your priors? Or is it more along the lines of, 'I strongly believe this is the correct interpretation,' and then you just adjust the descriptor as new information comes along?" Well, I think that you're supposed to think in terms of percentages, and ideally you would. It's actually notoriously difficult. Like, it's kind of not a simple calculation to be good about Bayes' theorem. What's relatively simple is to say this piece of information causes me to increase my credences in some things, decrease them in others. But the mathematical complication comes in because you have to make sure that all of your credences at the end of the day still add up to one, 100%, right? I mean, it's just a little bit of extra arithmetic. It's not terrible, but it's something that is tedious and we generally don't do it. And I certainly don't do it. So there's sort of a rolling update, I would say, as you're looking at more information and more facts about the world and thinking about how they all fit together, some credences go up, some go down. When I say things like being a good Bayesian, what I mean is think again about what we said before about string theory and the cosmological constant. It is too easy for people to say something like, "I think string theory is on the right track. I don't know whether string theory is compatible with a positive cosmological constant or not. Therefore, when we discovered the accelerating universe, it did not change my credences in string theory." I think that's kind of a mistake. I think that maybe it's permissible to have a positive cosmological constant in string theory, but I think in 1997, before we found the accelerating universe, it's not what you would have predicted. So I think it's okay and I think it's better to say, "My credences went down a little bit." Even if they were 99.99, they wouldn't have gone down that much. So maybe now they're 99.98, right? It doesn't affect your life in any way. It doesn't kick you out of the field or whatever. But you have to be honest. I think that Bayes' theorem is less a calculational necessity on a day-to-day basis and more a reality check and a way of keeping you honest about how information should change your beliefs about the world.

segments.questionText: I am struck by the number of interests I seem to share with you, a well-crafted cocktail, mechanical watches, reading a book with a cat purring softly on your lap. I have a hypothesis that there's a set of aesthetic preferences that correlate highly with interest in science and philosophy. This makes a testable prediction. Imagine designing your ideal car. I predict that it will have a dark forest green exterior with a supple dark saddle brown interior. How close was I?
segments.answerText: I would say you're medium close. I'm a little skeptical of your hypothesis overall because I know a lot of people that have interests in both science and philosophy, indeed in almost exactly the same kinds of science and philosophy that I do, but who have very different aesthetic interests and preferences than I do. So I'm not sure the data back you up. I mean, given that we share interests in cocktails and watches and cats and books, maybe that extends to other aesthetic preferences, but I don't think that the science and philosophy thing is quite the right direction to point on. The car question is difficult because I don't really have an imaginary ideal car. I think I could imagine myself being happy in all sorts of different cars, to be perfectly honest. I did for a while, when we were living in LA, have a Jaguar XK8 convertible that I loved to pieces. It kind of fell apart there at the end, but it had over 100,000 miles. It wasn't like it fell apart very early. A Jaguar is not the kind of car that you're gonna drive for 500,000 miles. So it was at its natural lifespan point when I traded it in. But it was lovely. And Jaguar, of course, famously... The classic Jaguars often came in this Jaguar Racing Green color. So the idea of a green exterior convertible car is very appealing to me for that reason more than the fact that I like green in general. But green in general is good. Brown interior, I'm not so sure. I might go with the black interior. So that's a slight data point that should decrease your credence in your hypothesis just a little bit.

segments.questionText: To what extent can we think of the entire large-scale structure of the universe, including great walls and galaxy superclusters billions of light-years away, as it all exists now? If every moment is relative to the observer and there's no God's-eye view from outside the universe and we can only see past light-cone slices, does it even make sense to think that what I would be able to see with if I had a God's-eye view of the entire universe?
segments.answerText: It does absolutely make sense to think of that. It doesn't make sense to assign some preference to one way of slicing the universe into moments of time. There's a slight preference 'cause cosmology does give you a rest frame of the universe, right? The frame at which you are at rest... Sorry, the frame with respect to which you're at rest to the cosmic microwave background and galaxies and things like that. But you can slice the universe into slices of constant time in different ways according to the rules of general relativity. So if you could imagine the God's-eye view, it would be a four-dimensional view. You'd be imagining the universe throughout all of space and all of time. You can't see it, right? You can't immediately, as a real non-God person, imagine experiencing that. But in science, all the time we take the observations that we do have and we construct pictures based on them. So there's nothing wrong with constructing a picture of what the universe looks like right now, even though we can't see it right now. We need to recognize that our picture might not be accurate, but that's also always true. That's not anything remarkably special about the universe or general relativity.

segments.questionText: How do you document your research progress for personal usage? Do you create slides as you go, or write LaTeX documents, or write in notebooks by hand?
segments.answerText: Yeah, I should have grouped this one with the thing about how I record the podcast 'cause, as usual, it's a mess. Things have changed for me since the invention of the Apple Pencil, okay? So there's a program... I experimented with different programs, I eventually landed on Notability is the one I use. And so Notability on my iPad is what I use for a lot of work in different ways. I use it to write my lecture notes for my classes. I use it to read PDF papers 'cause I can mark them up and take notes on them, as well as... You know, I have other documents. When I'm teaching a class, I have the photo roster of people in the class and things like that. So it's been super-duper useful. Taking notes of a good seminar or something like that. And then I can also file them, right? I can... You know, you can have the papers and my own notes in the same filing system and I can look at them and find them, which is kind of difficult. But that's just personal. For my papers that I write, most of my papers are written with my students and my collaborators, and we use a hodgepodge of different things. We are usually writing our LaTeX documents using Overleaf, which is the standard way of sharing LaTeX documents, which is the scientific typesetting system. I've also... I've recently, it took me a while since coming to Johns Hopkins, but I finally built up a good-sized research group. And so we're moving into the modern era where we use Slack to communicate like real businesses do. And we have a Zotero, which is a way of organizing papers, PDF files, and web pages that they come from. And again, you can organize them by topic and things like that. So hopefully this will supercharge our research progress in different ways. We'll see how that goes. But, again, for the most part, it's kind of haphazard and I have all sorts of different ways. I certainly don't create slides as I go. I try to create written documents when I have ideas that are half-baked. But again, sometimes that happens more effectively than others.

segments.questionText: Back in the 2000s, I started watching the NBA and playing NBA Live and fell in love with Vince Carter's game. He used to dunk on people left and right and have 30-foot game-winners and simply dominate basketball games in a way that I've seen no player do. Ever since then, I started training to dunk and still do more than 20 years later, and I saw over a thousand of his games. I'm wondering if there's a similar story for you with Dr. J. Did you like Dr. J for similar reasons? Did you follow his career? Can you relate to my story?
segments.answerText: Yeah, I can relate to that story. I do think that one of the great things about basketball in particular, but also just sports in general, is that you root for a team, but you get to know the players, right? You get to know something about the individuals, especially in this day and age. Like, you have no idea what it was like in the '70s and '80s without the internet. It was just much harder to get information on what the team was doing, what the players were like, and things like that. Now they all have their Instagram accounts, which are super boring. I don't follow any athletes on their Instagram accounts. But yeah, I mean, Dr. J was purchased by the Philadelphia 76ers in 1976, I think, when the American Basketball Association folded into the NBA. And the New Jersey Nets, who I think were the New York Nets at the time and are now the Brooklyn Nets, had to raise money to join the NBA, and they did so by selling Dr. J to the Philadelphia 76ers. So I was around 10 years old at the time, just getting interested in sports, so that was one of the first news stories in sports that I noticed. And I liked basketball right away. It was fast-paced and fun and athletic, and the Sixers were good. If I had started a few years earlier, the Sixers had one of the worst, I think the worst seasons in the history of the NBA. So maybe my story would have been very different. But Dr. J was great for several reasons. I mean, he was a great ambassador for the game. This was universally recognized. He sort of personally kept the ABA afloat for several years, and it was a huge coup when the NBA finally got him. He was well-spoken and had relationships with the fans that were really, really good. He was not a jerk like some players are. But also he was a winner. As soon as he got to the Sixers, they went to the NBA Finals. And I think he was with the Sixers for what, 10 years between getting there and retiring, and they went to the finals four times and they won once, which is a pretty good track record overall for anyone. I like to point to 1980, when he took the Sixers to the finals and literally no one else on the team was an All-Star except for Dr. J. I think that his ability to impact winning is a little bit underappreciated by the modern basketball fans. It was a different time in terms of statistics, so he doesn't have the gaudy numbers that a lot of modern players have. And there were no three-point shots, but he did a little bit of everything. He played defense really well. He got blocks and steals and rebounds and assists in addition to scoring. So that was very... I liked that aspect of him. But then, of course, the final thing is it was beautiful. He had the most aesthetically pleasing basketball game of anyone I've ever seen until the present day. He would dunk, he would run, and he would jump very high. And he was one of those... Very much like Vince Carter, he was one of those players where it looked like he would jump and then instead of coming down, he would start accelerating and keep going up again. And you know that's an optical illusion. I know the laws of physics don't really allow for that, but it looked like that. And he would not only have the dunks, he would have all of these twisty moves and finger rolls and acrobatic plays that just made it very pleasurable. You knew that at least once a game, Dr. J would bust out something that just made the whole audience gasp. The Sixers got better attendance on the road than they did at home because everyone wanted to see Dr. J. And by the end of the game, the other team's fans would be rooting for the Sixers because the Sixers had Dr. J. And it was just a very good side to be on as a young basketball fan getting to know the game.

segments.questionText: I think I mostly understand and am on board with your moral justification for eating animals, the fact that they can't imagine and be sad about a future where they are dead. But I want to try to push against it a bit. Imagine if someone went out and painlessly murdered a bunch of kittens. These kittens aren't anyone's pet, and no other beings will be adversely affected by their deaths. Based on your moral reasoning, would the action of killing the kittens not be morally reprehensible? The more fundamental question I'm getting at is, is there any special inherent moral value to life?
segments.answerText: So in my view, in my personal picture here, there's not any... The way to think about it is not by saying things like there's any special inherent moral value to life. And I think that your thought experiment actually indicates this very clearly because there are people who painlessly murder bunches of kittens, namely people who work at animal shelters where there's abandoned cats and dogs and they can't find homes for them. And those people are doing a morally good thing, right? They're saving these animals from really kind of miserable lives. And it's a shame that it has to happen. It would be better to imagine a hypothetical world where every cat found a good home. And I've done my part to help find kittens good homes, but there's too many kittens out there. And that's very different than if someone just murdered kittens, even if they did it painlessly, just because it gave them a thrill, right? Just because they kind of liked murdering kittens. That, I would judge as morally wrong in my own personal view, because that's a different thing. You're not doing it for some greater good. You're doing it for a not very good part of yourself. And so I think that it matters why you do it. And I think that all these are very complicated and I don't have strong feelings about any of them. Well, I have strong feelings, but I don't have strong convictions about my feelings. I'm willing to hear arguments on different sides. But we're all gonna die. Death happens to everybody. And so I don't think that death is the moral wrong. The reason why you force someone to die or you bring about the death of a person or an animal matters a lot. So that's why I say from the start, the right way to think about it is not, "Oh, there is special inherent moral value to life that we have to preserve." I think that's not dissimilar from the right answer, but it is not the best possible way to think about it.

segments.questionText: In the concept of a quantum cyclical universe, does each iteration consist of the same rules and constants?
segments.answerText: Well, different people have different models. So the recent model that I proposed with Sakshi Dulani and Nadia Diachenko is different than everybody else's model in a very specific way. Like most people who have cyclic models of cosmology, they're not periodic models. So they go through a cycle, but each cycle is a little bit different. And it depends on the model whether the rules are the same and the constants are the same. I think that in the space of actual models that actual people have actually written down, usually the rules and the constants are the same in a cyclical universe cosmology. I can imagine examples where they wouldn't be. I can absolutely imagine theories where that wouldn't be the case. But you have to ask yourself, why are you inventing this? Like, what is your motivation for trying to construct such a model? We had a very clear motivation for constructing our model, which is we wanted to know whether or not you could have a quantum cosmology based on a vector evolving. Unitarily, smoothly, in Hilbert space, in a finite-dimensional Hilbert space, without running into a Boltzmann brain problem. And we found a very specific, delicately chosen loophole that allowed us to do that. So we had a question we wanted the answer to, and we found it. I think that, roughly speaking, cyclical models are often thought of as alternatives to multiverse kind of models. And therefore, people who like cyclical models generally are not trying to make the rules and constants different from cycle to cycle.

segments.questionText: In your Dark Matter, Dark Energy Great Courses lecture four, you mentioned that it is possible to assume all length scales are shrinking rather than space expanding, although you say making such an assumption is silly. I was wondering if one could test the hypothesis with a tabletop experiment comprising a pair of charged masses on a frictionless track such that their gravitational attraction is balanced by their electrical repulsion.
segments.answerText: No, one cannot test the hypothesis because it is not a hypothesis. There's no science in saying that you can assume all length scales are shrinking rather than space expanding. Those are simply two different descriptions of exactly the same physical theory. It's like saying taking two numbers and adding them together using base 10 versus using base 2. You're gonna get the same numerical answer for a quantity. It might be expressed typographically differently, but the number you get by doing addition is the same no matter what base you use. And that's exactly the same thing if you use coordinates where space is expanding versus things shrinking. So there's no possible experimental test you can do because they're not actually two different hypotheses.

segments.questionText: Do we have any theory on how dark matter interacts with a black hole? I'm guessing that even if dark matter falls into a black hole or is around a black hole, we don't know that it is there.
segments.answerText: Well, the theory... Yes, we do have a theory. The theory is that dark matter interacts with a black hole exactly the same way that ordinary matter does. Dark matter... Well, let's go backwards. One of the great things about gravity is that everything interacts with it in exactly the same way. In particular, different particles might move on different trajectories if they have different speeds. But any two particles, if they're starting with the same initial conditions, they can be made of different stuff, but they will move in exactly the same way. That's the principle of equivalence. So dark matter particles move in exactly the same way as ordinary matter particles do. Now, once you go from one particle to many, the story changes by a lot. The thing about black holes are they're very small, right? The black hole at the center of our galaxy might be big to most of us by our everyday standards. It might be a light-year across, but compared to the size of the galaxy, that's really, really tiny. And even if it's a million times the mass of the sun, the galaxy is 100 billion times the mass of the sun. So it's tiny even by mass standards. So what that means is that even if there's a lot of dark matter in the galaxy, very little of it ever comes close to the black hole, much less falls in. So therefore, there's not a lot of relevance to black holes from the dark matter. The dark matter basically mostly is far away from the black hole and stays that way. With ordinary matter, there's a huge difference, which is that ordinary matter feels the force of electromagnetism, and therefore two atoms or two molecules or even just two particles can bump into each other and lose energy by emitting a photon, the particle of electromagnetism. And that is a source of dissipation. That means losing energy. And when you lose energy, if you're a particle in a gravitational potential, you fall toward the center. So the thing is that all that dissipation that ordinary matter has allows the ordinary matter to move in the direction of the black hole and to fall into it and to increase its size. As far as we can tell, and there's actually good constraints on this, dark matter doesn't have any dissipation. Dark matter doesn't interact with electromagnetism by the nature that it's dark, okay? Therefore, it doesn't lose energy, it doesn't fall into black holes. Now, I did once write a paper with some collaborators called Dark Matter and Dark Radiation, where we imagined a theory where dark matter has its own version of electromagnetism. And that might change the story a little bit, but only a little bit, because to make the story work, the dark matter needed to be very heavy and heavy enough that it wouldn't actually bump into other dark matter that much and lose energy. So we think that most of what goes into making a black hole is ordinary matter, just because it's easier to squeeze ordinary matter into small regions, whereas dark matter stays large and puffy.

segments.questionText: My 14-year-old would like to know why increased motion through space causes decreased motion through time. I could get as far as explaining that it's a feature of spacetime geometry per special relativity. But beyond that, I thought I'd consult an expert. Is there anything more fundamental to say, or is this a brute fact, or do we simply not know?
segments.answerText: Well, there's an underlying brute fact, but there's different ways of stating the brute fact. And this is a general feature of brute facts. When you say that some chain of explanation bottoms out in brute facts, it's often the case that you're allowed to choose different brute facts as your explanations. It's exactly like saying a given axiomatic system in geometry or logic or number theory, you can replace some axioms for others and get exactly the same system overall. So for something like spacetime... Think of it this way. Let's just start with the idea that spacetime has a geometry. And let's ignore general relativity and complications of curvature of geometry. Let's imagine the geometry is flat. Let's make our lives easy. In that case, every dimension of spacetime comes with two options, either the spacetime interval along it is positive or it's negative, or it's zero. But usually we choose things so that the zero direction is some combination of positive and negative, and the fundamental directions like X, Y, Z, and T all have a positive sign associated with them or a negative sign. So the brute fact is the distribution of positive and negative signs in the spacetime interval that is appropriate to spacetime. In Euclidean geometry, all the spacetime intervals are positive, and therefore the shortest distance between any two points is a straight line, because by deviating in any direction, you add more and more to your spacetime interval. It so happens the brute fact is that we live in a spacetime where what we call time has a negative number in front of it for the spacetime interval, and all the other spatial directions have a positive number. Now, in fact, that's a convention. You could have done it the other way. You could have given the positive number to time and the negative number to the spatial directions. But they have to be opposite. That's the important thing. And because they're the opposite, you have an option of moving in space or moving in time. And if you move a little bit in space but come back to where you started, you will always experience less time. The deviation in space adds the opposite amount of spacetime interval than the deviation in time. And that's the brute fact that you have to deal with. And you're always allowed to ask, could it have been different? Are there reasons why? People have tried to have more than one dimension of time, have negative spacetime intervals with more than one dimension. It generally doesn't work. Generally bad things happen and most people are not encouraged. But there's always some people who are really into the idea and they push it, and so they're thinking about things like that. But no reason to get too excited about it just right now.

segments.questionText: In your recent podcast with Vitor Cardoso, he said, 'Whereas black holes, because gravitational collapse acts so efficiently, it just cleans them of any detail or of any other detail. They're really just simple curled up vacuum.' Could you elaborate on this? Where does the matter of the collapsing star go? Is it all the energy converted to gravitational energy and pressure, which then drives the curvature so that light can no longer escape?
segments.answerText: I encourage people to check out the books I've written about things like this, such as Space, Time and Motion, or even, I think, back in From Eternity to Here, I talked about this thing. The thing is, the matter doesn't go anywhere in some very real sense up until the point where it hits the singularity. When a star collapses to make a black hole, you can think of at any moment of time, if you think about four-dimensional spacetime and then slicing it into different moments of constant time, that slice will always hit the star. The star will get smaller and smaller, but it will never hit zero size at any one moment of time in the usual way of slicing spacetime into moments of time. Now, if you fall into the black hole and you say, "I want to go hit the star," you might not be able to do that. In fact, very, very rapidly, you will reach a point where you're too late and you're gonna hit the singularity, which is in your future before you hit the star. So there's no way to measure how big the star is in some very real sense, but maybe you can see the light emitted by it or something like that. But nothing magical happens inside the black hole. I think that when someone like Vitor says gravitational collapse acts so efficiently, it just, it's nothing but simple curled up vacuum, there's two things going on. One is when we first study black hole spacetimes in our general relativity class, it's too complicated to think about a real star collapsing. We just think about an eternal black hole that was always there and has no matter associated with it. This is the eternal Schwarzschild vacuum solution. That's perfectly legitimate. It's not representing the real world. In the real world, black holes come about because of stars collapsing. The eternal Schwarzschild solution has all sorts of weird properties. It has not only a black hole, but it has a white hole in the past out of which things can come but nothing can go in. And it also has a wormhole connecting a whole other copy of the universe. One asymptotically flat spacetime is connected to another one by the Schwarzschild wormhole, which was invented by Einstein, Podolsky, and Rosen in their EPR paper... Sorry, not Einstein, Podolsky, and Rosen, Einstein and Rosen without Podolsky in their ER paper, the Einstein-Rosen bridge, which is where this wormhole idea came from. But the Einstein-Rosen bridge and the white hole are not thought to really exist in the world, but we study them because there's a simple mathematical setup to look at first. And the other thing going on is that even if you do know that in the real world black holes are made by collapsing matter, the exterior of the black hole is the same in the version where it was made by collapsing matter as it was in the simple mathematical idealization without any matter. So you can start thinking of it in exactly the same way. That was why it's worth your time to study the simple Schwarzschild black hole without any matter in it. The point is that the Schwarzschild solution lets you describe a black hole without any matter creating it, but we think that real-world black holes are created by matter, but the end result looks exactly the same either way. So I think that's what's going on in that description.

segments.questionText: In a recent podcast, the guest used the term 'fractal-like' in the same way that I'm used to hearing you use 'scale-free.' Is there anything interesting to say about the difference?
segments.answerText: Probably not. They're very closely related. I would say that fractals are scale-free in some sense. That's one way of saying what fractal is supposed to mean. I think that fractal has a more narrow definition. A fractal is a kind of a geometric figure, right? It is something that has a shape or something like that. The coast of Norway is fractal at some resolution, but there's all these curves you can construct mathematically that are infinitely fractal all the way down to zero size. And so they're scale-free in the sense that if you take a fractal and you zoom in on it, the statistical properties of the little subset that you're looking at are the same as the statistical properties of the fractal as a whole. That's what it means to be scale-free. But if I say that the distribution of, I don't know, city populations follows a power law, power laws are scale-free. There's no preferred size, there's just a relative size. If you're twice as big, then you appear half as often or something like that. So it's a more general notion. So fractals are a subset of scale-free behavior, I guess I would say. And I don't want people necessarily thinking of some pointy, sharp geometric figure when I say that some relationship is a power law and therefore scale-free.

segments.questionText: a priority question. "Some people have suggested that time may not really exist." Oh no, what kind of people would do that?" After reading From Eternity to Here and listening to Mindscape, it is relatively easy to understand how the arrow of time may be an artifact and time passing may be an illusion created by our brains. But the fact remains, it takes different times for things to happen. Have you any idea how people who suggest time may not exist explain that other than time does exist?
segments.answerText: " Yeah, again, I should have grouped this with the earlier one, but the point is time has to emerge. The people who say time doesn't exist should, if they're intellectually consistent, say that tables and chairs don't exist either. And there are people who say that, and those people deserve your pity, not your contempt. It's just hard to go through life not believing in tables and chairs or the existence of time, okay? You can think that time is not fundamental, but chairs are not fundamental either. That's okay, they still exist, right? Again, just like the ability of human beings to make choices, whatever you want to call it, the ability to travel into the future by letting time pass is something that is indubitably real. It definitely exists. So I think that people who say that time doesn't really exist are literally just thinking or using words in sloppy ways, let's put it that way. Just tell them to show up at some time and see how well they do. If they're able to show up at the right time, they must be fibbing to you when they say that time doesn't exist.

segments.questionText: In the last AMA, you made the perhaps unintentionally provocative statement that what we call the electron neutrino and what we call the electron are basically the same, with their differences arising from symmetry breaking. This felt like one of the 'Professor Sean lifts the fog' conceptual breakthroughs I've experienced decades after graduating with a physics degree. I'd appreciate some elaboration. Is this related to the question of whether related particles such as electrons and positrons are not fundamentally separate entities, but different excitations of a common underlying field?
segments.answerText: Yeah, it's related to that, but it's also a little bit different than that. So, I mean, electrons and neutrinos are not the same story as electrons and positrons, okay? But in both cases, you have different components of some kind of underlying field. The difference is with the electrons and the neutrinos, if you think about before the symmetry is broken, so you think about before electroweak symmetry breaking, before the Higgs boson got a non-zero value in empty space. The Higgs boson in the sufficiently early universe, the Higgs field had an expectation value of zero. So it was sitting there, not doing anything. And in that case, there is a two-dimensional field which you could call the electron/neutrino field. And it's like... It's literally, think of a plane, right, with two directions on it. And there's no difference between going in one direction and going in the other direction. After the symmetry is broken, what the Higgs field does is basically, it makes a valley. So if you're... If you have some physics background, imagine that your plane is given coordinates X and Y. And there's no intrinsic difference between X and Y. You could rotate your coordinates. It just doesn't matter. There's no such thing as which is the electron, which is the neutrino. It was just two directions somewhere in the plane. But then someone adds a potential energy to the plane. And there is a coordinate system, X and Y, such that the potential energy is Y squared, which means that if I move in the X direction, there's no potential at all. But suddenly, if I move in the Y direction, now it costs me potential energy. And that X direction, ex post facto, is what we call the neutrino. It's nearly massless, no potential. And the Y direction is what we call the electron. It costs energy to move in that direction, which we interpret as the mass of the electron. And the previous rotational symmetry that we had in the plane has been broken by the existence of that potential energy. And this is exactly, this is not even an analogy. This is just literally what the Higgs expectation value does. It treats one direction differently than the other one. And there was no inherent choice as to which direction was going to be treated differently. In fact, it's a gauge symmetry. So there's literally no fact of the matter about which direction was going to be treated differently. It's just a coordinate difference Whereas electrons and positrons, those are antiparticles, and those were always antiparticles, and those were always different. They're, again, part of the same Dirac field, if you want to think about it that way, but they were always pretty... The fact that they have opposite charges was always true, let's put it that way. Armchair epitomologist. I don't think this is a real word. It's not epidemiologist or epistemologist. Maybe the S is missing. It's epistemologist without an S, epitomologist. "Taking the simplistic model that human civilization's technological advancement is linear, something like the Kardashev scale, what sort of general credences do you put on our civilization progressing technologically versus regressing in the next thousand years, 10k years, 100k years, et cetera? I know it's not a fully specified question and obviously impossible to know, but I'm curious of your general degree of belief in our civilization to achieve these sci-fi levels of technological advancement before we're wiped out or sent back to the Stone Age by ourselves or some external factors, or maybe we just get stuck at around our current stage." I think this is fun stuff to think about. I think that we don't have any right to be especially confident in our thoughts about this. And back when we were talking about how do you detect the crackpots, acting super confident about questions like this is a kind of a signal of crackpottery right there, because we don't know. It's like acting like you know what happened at the Big Bang. Like, you might have theories and you should take them seriously, but you shouldn't be too wedded to them. I think two things are simultaneously true that make it very, very difficult to answer this question. One thing is that the advance of technology has given human beings powers that they didn't have before. You know, back in the days of 100,000 years ago, there weren't that many human beings on the earth compared to how many there are now, but the ability of any one human being to do damage to the entire rest of humanity was negligible, right? Like, how many other people could you hurt before they stopped you? Not that many. The ability of technology has given individual human beings an outsized potential influence on the rest of the world. We obviously now as a species, we can change the whole environment of the planet, right? Like, we're doing it. It's very noticeable. But also between nuclear weapons and biological weapons and various internet-based technological things, there's a whole bunch of things that human beings can do that have an outsized impact on the world in which we live. So that raises the risk level of what humanity can do to itself in an unprecedented way. That's one thought that makes it difficult to predict the future. The other side has the fact that complex systems tend to be resilient. Like an individual complex system, like a human being, is not that difficult to kill. Chop off a head, usually you kill it. But complex systems as a whole that are distributed in all sorts of different ways, very, very difficult to completely wipe out. In fact, it's hard. Despite the fact that we have nuclear weapons and all this stuff, it's actually not easy to come up with a scenario where human beings, even if we tried, could literally kill off all the human beings on Earth. We can imagine creating diseases that kill off a lot of people, or having a nuclear war that kills an enormous amount of people, like really tremendous tragedies. But the chances that some human beings would survive are still quite high even in those relatively extreme situations. And so both of these are very fuzzy, right? On the one hand, we're saying we can have a huge impact on the planet. On the other, we're saying we're pretty plucky. And neither one of those is anywhere close to specific enough to make predictions for what's gonna happen the next thousand years, 10,000 years, et cetera. I will also say that human beings are terrible at timescales. We're good at imagining things. We're very bad at imagining how long something will take. So I think that the fact that we can build rocket ships and things like that now has caused some people to think about going to Mars or going to the moon or whatever, colonizing the solar system. It's pretty easy to write science fiction novels about this. It's really hard to do it in practice. We had the podcast with Zach and Kelly Wienersmith where they explained some of the obstacles to that in very clear terms. And the thing is, the people who tend to be most interested in these questions also tend to be most invested in making it happen, so they're not always the most realistic. So in 10,000 years from now, I would not be at all surprised if there were plenty of human beings living off of the Earth somewhere. 100 years from now, I would be very surprised if there were a lot of human beings living off the Earth. There'll be a few. There are a few right now, if you count living in the space station. But timescales are hard. And think about what you would have said about the future a thousand years ago and how wrong you would have been. Well, we'll probably be just as wrong if we try to predict what the future is like a thousand years from now. So I'm optimistic about the ability of humanity to adapt. I am pessimistic about our ability to say what that would actually mean in terms of what things will be like even a thousand years from now, much less 100,000.

segments.questionText: Can you shed light on the relation between symmetries and the laws of physics? Is it just an aspect of the math, or are there philosophical reasons why a broken symmetry must mean there is a particle in the universe?
segments.answerText: So I got confused. I thought I was following you there, Jeroen, in the first half of the question, symmetries and the laws of physics. But why a broken symmetry must mean there is a particle in the universe, I'm not quite sure what that is pointing at. I'm gonna guess that what you mean is the Higgs phenomenon, which we were just talking about a second ago. The Higgs mechanism is a very specific kind of symmetry breaking. It's not the general idea of symmetry breaking, which is quite general and powerful, nor is it the general idea of symmetries, full stop. The Higgs field is... The Higgs phenomenon, I should say, the Higgs mechanism is a particular way to break a symmetry because a field takes on a non-zero value in empty space. And this goes back to Brout and Englert and Higgs and others. Philip Anderson sort of had a premonition of it beforehand. You can break a symmetry by a field having a value. It's exactly like this. Imagine you have a circle and you say, well, all the... Or a sphere is even better. Imagine you have a two-dimensional sphere, the surface of a ball, and it's perfectly smooth and there's no distinguishing features on it. It's perfectly symmetric. But you pick randomly a point to call the North Pole and the South Pole that you're gonna rotate it around. You have broken the symmetry, by picking out those preferred points on the sphere. They weren't picked out as preferred ahead of time. So you need something to break the symmetry, and the Higgs field is what breaks it in quantum field theory, in the Standard Model of particle physics. And so it's not that breaking a symmetry means there must be a particle. It's that this particular symmetry breaking mechanism involves a quantum field taking on a non-zero value. And whenever you have a field, you have a particle, because particles are just vibrations in fields. Now, there's a deeper question that I thought you were getting into in the first part of your question, why are the laws of physics as we know them full of symmetries? That's maybe even too deep for me to really give a sensible answer to. I certainly think it's possible that the symmetries that we see in the laws of physics are kind of an artifact. They're kind of a reflection of how we as human beings find it easiest to describe what is going on. Just like, again, with the sphere, maybe we have different directions of space and they're all equal in some way, and so we invent a mathematical representation of this where there's a representation that acts like a rotation and gives us a different view, but it's the same underlying stuff, so we call it a symmetry. Okay. So whether or not the laws of physics really love symmetry very much, or whether or not we human beings love symmetry very much because it helps us describe the laws of physics, I think is a good question to which I don't have a perfect answer right now.

segments.questionText: I'm sad that LeBron James didn't join the Warriors. I take comfort that we have Steph Curry, and one could argue that in basketball, philosophy, and physics, and other endeavors, one's ability to change the game may be more important than stats. Do you agree that Steph Curry is more of a game changer than LeBron? And do you think that the greatest strides in physics and philosophy are made by game changers or those who have great stats, e.g., they publish a lot?
segments.answerText: Well, Carmaria, I think that the analogy is a little bit strained, actually. I don't think that the changing the game versus publishing a lot is really quite the right distinction to draw. Look, I've said this before. I'm not a believer that you can rank basketball players or athletes or scientists, for that matter, in some objective criteria of excellence once and for all. I think that you can look at what they did. You could look at the championships they've won, the statistics they've accumulated, the ways in which they've helped their teams and things like that. I think that what you're getting at is LeBron James, as amazing as he is, the things he's done are kind of things that other people have done in the past. He's just doing them better. Whereas Steph Curry really did something that no one else had ever done before in his particular way of playing the game and changing the game. Just being able to shoot so quickly, being able to move around the court so quickly that he could get open to shoot even though he's not especially tall and everyone knew that he was gonna shoot. And to make these wild shots from a long way away at absurdly high efficiency was a different kind of excellence than someone like LeBron James has. I mean, LeBron in many ways is somewhere in between Michael Jordan and Magic Johnson, right? He has the scoring chops, but he also has the passing chops. He's a tall point guard kind of player like Magic was, but a very efficient scoring machine like Michael Jordan was. But those are predecessors, right? It's harder to find an obvious predecessor for Steph Curry. I think they're both important. I don't think that greater strides are made by one or the other. I think at the end of the day, it's who wins the game. At the end of the day, it's what discoveries were made by what scientist and how they went about doing it. The greatness or the lack of greatness is less interesting to me than what was actually accomplished.

segments.questionText: I saw you on the Lives Well Lived podcast earlier in August and it was quite an unusual one with those questions on morality of the many worlds, among other things. I was wondering if we should even ask such questions, like the morality of many worlds interpretation, or any theory of physics for that matter. How did you feel the talk went? Was it time well spent?
segments.answerText: Yes, you might remember that we had Peter Singer here on the Mindscape podcast. And Peter has his own podcast called Lives Well Lived and he invited me on, so I appeared on that. And I think it went pretty well from my perspective. It was a weird mixture because Peter Singer doesn't care about the philosophy of physics. He cares about ethics and morality more than anything else. And so he kind of wanted to talk about that, but he had me on, so he also talked about physics.
