He asked me some questions about many worlds. And he has a... I'm sorry, I should look this up. I'm not gonna look it up right now because I'm in the middle of doing the AMA. But he has a co-podcaster, I'm sorry, I forgot her name, but she did as much talking and we had a three-way conversation. It was great. What I guess I was happiest about was that he didn't point out any obvious mistakes to me in my own moral philosophy, even though we completely disagree. I think that when we got to talking about moral philosophy, even though we had different takes on it, I still, coming out of it, agreed with my own reasoning more than his, right? Sometimes when you talk to someone really smart who you know disagrees with you, you have this crisis of confidence moment where you start thinking like, "Oh my God, what if they're right? What if their arguments... I haven't thought about that one. They clearly know this better than I do." So I didn't have that with Peter Singer. That could be a flaw in me. Maybe the better arguments were there and I've just lost the ability to hear them, so entrenched am I in my worldview. But I don't have that impression coming out. But I do think that I was happy with how I did defend my own views, and hopefully some people got something out of the conversation, which I thought was indeed time well spent.

segments.questionText: My interpretation of your description of emergence makes me worry for the long-term mental health of Laplace's demon. Am I right to do so? My take is that they would either have no necessity for considering such constructions as trees, cats, and humans useful, so the universe would seem entirely mundane, or they would find in any arbitrary collection of matter equally useful and become befuddled by the variation. Should we set up a GoFundMe page in anticipation of their future needs?
segments.answerText: Well, the good news is Laplace's demon doesn't care about those things, so their mental health is not in any danger. But your intuition is correct. Laplace's demon... There's different versions of the thought experiment, but you can certainly imagine a completely self-consistent and self-contained version of Laplace's demon that never knows the notions of trees or cats or humans or entropy or temperature or classical physics or anything like that. They just solve the wave function of the universe once and for all and that's it. They have an exact description of the entire world and they don't need to think about any of the emergent levels. That's completely allowed. But Laplace's demon doesn't exist, so don't set up any GoFundMe pages. If you do see any out there, they're probably just scams.

segments.questionText: In your recent conversation with Chandra Sripada, you said his arguments shifted your credences about whether LLMs have rediscovered some of the ways humans think. I'm curious where your credences are now. Given your views on emergence and levels of description, to what extent do you think that today's most capable LLMs exhibit intelligence or cognition in something like the same sense that humans do? At the emergent level where we actually recognize and evaluate intelligence, do you now think differences in substrate and lower-level mechanism become less important than the higher-level regularities that the two systems share? You mentioned convergent evolution. Might the similarities arise because prediction has shaped both systems, humans through direct interaction with the world as well as culture and language, and LLMs indirectly through the enormous cultural record humans have produced from that interaction?
segments.answerText: Well, the thing at the end about prediction shaping both systems is exactly Chandra's point. That's what he wants to hypothesize is actually happening here. But I want to separate this issue from the issue of silicon versus biology, okay? That may or may not become important to questions of consciousness, and we'll get to that in the very next question. But cognition was what Chandra was thinking about. And cognition is much simpler in some sense. It's just reasoning, just thinking, just adding numbers together, making decisions, things like that. It's not conscious experience or any such thing. So the question with LLMs always was the following. They're not built, they're not architected or designed to mimic the actual structures in the human brain, okay? They don't have a cerebellum and frontal cortex and all that stuff. Their architecture is inspired by the idea of neurons and how they talk to each other, but they're not wired together in some hierarchical way relative to what the human brain is doing. Instead, they are trained to give outputs based on inputs that resemble what human beings would do. And so the open question always is, did LLMs manage to accurately mimic what human beings would do by rediscovering the way human beings do them, or by discovering a new way to do really similar things? And there's good arguments on both sides, right? Some arguments for the similarities come from just the similarities of the inputs and the outputs. Some arguments for the differences come from the fact that when LLMs do make mistakes, there's sort of a characteristic kind of mistake that they make that human beings wouldn't make, that indicates that they're reasoning differently in some ways. And so I think it's an interesting open question. And I've often said this, and people said, "Oh no, they clearly have rediscovered human ways of thinking," but all of their evidence was just... They sound human at the end of the day. That's what it always came down to, or they're really smart. But it was the kind of smartness that was under question, not the existence of their smartness. And I thought that Chandra gave a good job of at least making an argument that we have evidence that the way in which they're thinking is closely related to that of humans. Now, others strongly disagree with this, right? This is not a consensus view by any stretch. There is no consensus view about this, but I was glad to see some real evidence put forward. I think that it's just the beginning of us understanding this. I don't think that we're close to figuring out once and for all the similarities or differences between humans and LLMs. As Chandra readily admits, you need a lot more input, you need a lot more tokens to train your LLM to give those human-like responses. And that's kind of obvious why. It's namely because human brains have structure in them that LLMs are not born with. So that's an important difference. So I don't think it's... All of that discussion is completely aside from the question of silicon versus biology or anything like that. But it's very, very interesting to imagine that the way that we human beings go about cogitating, as optimized by natural selection and the ability, the desire to make accurate predictions, turns out via convergent evolution to be similar to the way that LLMs go about reasoning. I don't have strong feelings one way or the other, but I'm absolutely open to the evidence pushing us in one direction or the other.

segments.questionText: that, "Chandra said you used to lean functionalist about consciousness, but you might have drifted away from it. Where do you actually stand now? Did his mechanistic case pull you back at all, or are you still leaning towards something like Anil Seth's biological naturalism?
segments.answerText: " So I'm on neither side. So number one, Chandra was not talking about consciousness. We were not talking about consciousness in that podcast. We were talking about cognition, which is something different. And number two, Anil Seth and also Ned Block, we recently had on the podcast, have made cases against computational functionalism as a way of thinking about consciousness without giving up on physicalism about consciousness. So again, I'm not pretending to be an expert on consciousness. I really promise you I am not. And part of my non-expertness was that I never quite appreciated that you could be a physicalist without being a computational functionalist. But there is a leap involved, and I think that Anil and Ned are both completely correct about this, that just because at the end of the day there's physical stuff moving around in different ways, obeying the laws of physics, that's not enough to make you instantly leap to thinking that whatever consciousness is, it's a matter of functional processing of information. There might be more to it than that, even if the more is still 100% physical, not weird, spooky, ineffable, spiritual stuff, right? So I think that's all. I think that's the only change that has happened in my conception of consciousness is that I have a greater appreciation for the difference conceptually in saying that you're a physicalist and saying you're a computational functionalist. So I'm open to the possibility that there are things going on which don't map on in any direct way to computation, but are going on in the human brain or human biology, just in the metabolic processes, the entropic gradients, whatever is going on in the brain that doesn't come across in a computational description, but is nevertheless important for consciousness. I'm open to that possibility. I'm very open to lots of things when it comes to consciousness as long as they're compatible with the laws of physics.

segments.questionText: What do you make of the growing movement to oppose the construction of data centers? There seems to be some elements of a moral panic, particularly around the idea they consume large amounts of water, mixed with some semi-legitimate NIMBY-esque objections about noise and aesthetics, all clouded by general anxiety about the future of AI.
segments.answerText: Yeah, I think that your reading is pretty similar to my own. I don't have strong opinions here one way or the other. It reminds me of a question we got a couple months ago in AMA about my feeling about the lab leak hypothesis for the origin of COVID-19. And I said, look, I don't care in some ways. That's not the case with data centers. For data centers, I care. For COVID, I didn't care. I don't care if it's natural origins or synthetic origins. What I care about is being honest and scientific about getting the answer. And it became very difficult to do that because people have so many non-epistemic values and interests that come into the discussion of these issues. And so I think the same thing is true with data centers. There's, on the one hand, there's an argument to be made that data centers are useful. On the other hand, there are absolutely legitimate arguments that they cause harm if they're done badly, right? That they cause pollution and that they're a waste of money and they run rampant over people's rights and lands and all these things. And it's just very, very difficult to have that conversation because the pro-data center side is entirely biased by money. They want to make money. They're going to tell you the data centers are good because if they build one, they'll make billions of dollars. And so it's kind of hard to take them at face value when they make those arguments. But the anti-data center side is also contaminated by semi-Luddite objections to the very ideas of technology and capitalism or whatever. And I think you need a nuanced discussion, and it's just hard to find nuanced discussions. So I don't dig very much into that myself. I don't get my hackles up about data centers pro or con. The one thing, I guess, that really does kind of rub me the wrong way is the gigantic imbalance of power between rich people and non-rich people in the country, right? If I had to pick a side, I would be, given that I'm not very up on the actual issues here, I would be predisposed to pick the side of the people who are not billionaires and trillionaires because their voices are harder to get heard, right? And so I would think that if you just listened to the voices out there, you're going to get a biased view in a very particular direction. But that's no way to make difficult decisions about public policy. So I think that it's weird to see, for example, the Democratic Party, which in many ways you might think would be anti-data center. And why would you think that? Well, number one, they want to preserve the environment. Number two, they want to oppose Republicans who are very pro-data center. And number three, data centers are really unpopular right now. So you might think, wow, this is a real obvious winner for Democratic politicians. And then you look at the actual positions of Democratic politicians, and many of them are very pro-data center. And you go, oh, my goodness, what's happening? Guess what's happening. They're getting lots of money in their campaign contributions from the companies who want to build data centers. So that huge amount of money, they just distort the discussion, the public dialogue around these things by quite a bit. And that does absolutely rub me the wrong way as much as any specific issue about using up water or whatever for the data centers.

segments.questionText: I'm curious what is the latest on your Physics of Democracy book and whether you'd be up to publish the course syllabus or reading list for the Physics of Democracy class that you taught?
segments.answerText: Yeah, I'm writing it, getting there. Progress is being made. I have a deadline. I'm rushing to meet it. It is quite a lot of work these days going into the Physics of Democracy book, but that means it will come out, that it'll be a success that way. You always wish you had more time, but sometimes it's good to have a deadline. It focuses your mind. I actually, precisely because I'm right in the throes of writing it, I would rather not say too much about it because it changes, right? This is what it's like to write things. You write things... I've written so many words that I've then deleted, right? Or I've moved chapters around, I've changed my opinions about important issues. I've written things pushing one point of view and then realized, no, actually I don't even agree with that point of view. I gotta change it. So I don't want to talk too much about that. When the book is all done, you'll know. And I think so far, so good. I'm having fun writing the book. I'm learning a lot. I'm liking how it's turning out. I need to restrain myself about getting into the technical weeds a little bit. There's no equations in this book. Even when I talk about power laws, I even use words like lognormal, but I don't define what it means. And that's just... It really hurts me. It really stabs me in the heart to not explain to you what a lognormal distribution looks like. But I feel I have to say it. Maybe my editor will take it out, but at the moment, that's where I am. I'm just trying to say things in a fun, sprightly, page-turning way that gets a lot of real physics and a lot of real political science across, even occasionally economics and computer science and philosophy, in ways that are compelling to everybody but still more or less accurate. I can already see that there's gonna be criticisms of the book no matter what I do. I had one discussion, I won't go into details, but as soon as you say physics of democracy, people are like, "Oh yeah, that's cool." And then they say, "You better include issue X, which is my hobby horse, and you need to talk about it in your book." Everyone's gonna have an issue X that they are very sad that I didn't talk about. And what can you do? I can encourage them to write their books. That's the best I can do. But it will come out. A year from now, maybe it'll be out. Who knows? We'll have to see. So thanks as always for listening this far in, for supporting the Mindscape podcast. The support means a lot to me. I will talk to you next time. Take care. [music]
